summary: Records, for the historical record, the motivation behind the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP). DCCP is an unreliable transport protocol with end-to-end congestion control, meant for applications such as streaming media and online games. The document is informational.

eli5.summary: Some programs, like games and live video, would rather skip a late message than wait for it. This explains why a new way of sending messages was invented that stays polite to the network without resending.

questions: what is the congestion control problem
why not use tcp for streaming
why not add congestion control to udp
subtitle: Why streaming media and games need a transport protocol with congestion control.

tldr.problem: Applications like streaming media and online games use UDP to avoid TCP's delays but do not implement congestion control, threatening Internet stability. Congestion control is difficult to implement correctly, and alternative approaches fall short.
tldr.mechanism: This problem statement argues that a new transport protocol combining unreliable datagram delivery with mandatory, built-in congestion control is the best solution. It should support multiple congestion control algorithms, explicit connection setup, and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN).
tldr.outcome: RFC 4340 defines DCCP as the standardized realization of these requirements, providing the first widely-specified alternative to TCP/UDP with congestion-controlled unreliable delivery.

today: RFC 4336 is Informational and documents the historical rationale for DCCP. DCCP was standardized in RFC 4340 (2006) and subsequent RFCs, but has seen limited real-world deployment. The reasons include the difficulty of modifying operating systems to add a new transport protocol, the preference of many applications for unreliable delivery without congestion control, and the availability of TCP-based solutions (e.g., media delivered over HTTPS) for many streaming scenarios. However, the problem statement remains valid: congestion control for unreliable flows remains an unsolved challenge in the Internet.

sections.title: The Congestion Control Problem
sections.content:
Historically, TCP carried most congested traffic on the Internet and implemented robust congestion control to avoid overloading networks. UDP carried mostly short, request-response traffic (DNS, SNMP) with little congestion impact. However, recent applications such as streaming audio, Internet telephony, and multiplayer games generate large, long-lived UDP flows that lack congestion control. Unlike TCP, which guarantees in-order, reliable delivery (useful when every bit matters), these applications prioritize timeliness: a message that arrives too late is worthless and should not be retransmitted.

As the volume of non-congestion-controlled UDP traffic grows relative to congestion-controlled TCP, the Internet faces real stability risks. Routing becomes congested, latency spikes, and TCP flows back off in response to loss, while UDP applications ignore the network's distress signals. Applications could implement their own congestion control, but experience shows this is difficult to get right, and most application developers prefer not to reinvent this wheel. A standardized, easy-to-use solution is needed.
sections.eli5: When everyone's TV buffers itself slower when the WiFi is busy, the internet stays healthy. But when everyone's TV ignores the WiFi load and just keeps streaming at full speed, everything gets congested and the TV picture breaks anyway.

sections.title: Why UDP Variants are Inadequate
sections.content:
A new protocol must support unreliable, congestion-controlled datagram delivery, but modifying UDP or layering congestion control above it creates problems. Congestion control implemented at the application layer places a burden on developers and makes it easy for applications to evade congestion control by modifying the code. Congestion control below UDP requires either the application to provide sequence numbers and feedback (duplicating effort) or a new protocol layer between IP and UDP (making packets unrecognizable as UDP to firewalls).

The RFC also examines whether to modify existing transport protocols: TCP's feedback mechanism is unsuitable for smooth-response algorithms like TFRC, and any TCP change takes years to standardize. SCTP was designed for reliable, multi-stream communication with streams and chunks that add header overhead unsuitable for audio packets. RTP is used by many applications but provides too much functionality for simple congestion-controlled flows. Rather than burdening these protocols with unreliable variants, a clean new protocol is the best answer.
sections.eli5: You can't just ask each app to handle congestion control itself — they get it wrong. You can't hide it below UDP — then firewalls won't recognize your packets. You can't modify TCP, SCTP, or RTP — they're built for different jobs. So you need something new and simple.

sections.title: Protocol Design Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC specifies requirements for a minimal transport protocol designed for congestion-controlled unreliable flow. It must mandate built-in congestion control to prevent applications from evading it. It must support multiple congestion control algorithms: at minimum, TCP-like congestion control (strict window reduction on loss) and TFRC (smooth rate reduction on loss). Applications need Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) support so routers can signal congestion without dropping packets, allowing the sender to react in advance. The protocol must use explicit connection setup and teardown handshakes to ease stateful firewall traversal and enable servers to protect against spoofed connection attacks.

To keep overhead low for small packets (a 14-byte audio packet should not carry a large header), the protocol should allow data on initial setup datagrams and minimize per-packet byte overhead. Features like reliability or forward error correction should be layered on top rather than built in. The protocol must reliably negotiate congestion control parameters so both endpoints agree on the algorithm and feedback mechanism.
sections.eli5: The protocol must be small and simple, let apps pick how to reduce speed, work with routers that signal congestion without dropping, and let firewalls see the connection setup.

sections.title: Practical Design Challenges
sections.content:
Beyond core congestion control, the RFC identifies several additional concerns: mobility and multihoming (mechanisms to handle devices moving between networks or having multiple paths) are not essential to the core problem and are omitted from the minimal design. Denial of Service protection requires careful connection setup and teardown to resist SYN-flood attacks and spoofed packets. Firewall and NAT traversal demand explicit handshakes and well-known port conventions. Interoperation with RTP (widely used by streaming applications) should be considered: the new protocol might suggest modifications to RTP, such as reduced headers that avoid duplication with the transport layer.

The protocol must define an API that allows applications to decide at transmission time what data to send (especially important for video and games where only the latest frame matters) and provide applications with sequence number information. The document emphasizes that many of these requirements come from real experience: a 1998 IETF working group on unicast transport requirements had identified unmet needs that this protocol should address.
sections.eli5: The protocol also has to deal with NAT and firewalls, protect against attacks, work with video apps, and let apps pick the newest data to send instead of old data waiting in a queue.

sections.title: Why Reluctant Applications Matter
sections.content: A key insight is that many applications using UDP prefer the lack of congestion control: they get better performance without it. For the new protocol to be widely adopted, it must be attractive to reluctant applications that would not use it otherwise. Design features supporting this include: offering multiple congestion control algorithms so applications can choose smooth or aggressive responses; providing ECN so applications see congestion signals and can adjust smoothly; and minimizing overhead so the protocol does not harm performance. The RFC acknowledges that some flows will remain uncongestion-controlled, and router-based penalty mechanisms (broadly termed penalty boxes) may eventually be needed to detect and penalize uncontrolled high-bandwidth flows during congestion, but the first step is to make congestion control easy and attractive.
sections.eli5: Apps would rather not use congestion control if they don't have to. So the new protocol needs to be so good that apps want to use it — offering choices, efficiency, and early warning of congestion.
